candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Genesis
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis, Section XVII.5. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13, ed. J. Gwynn / Schaff (1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham; for a father of many nations have I made thee'. Ephrem reads the divine name-change as a SACRAMENTAL renaming: the addition of the heh (the divine breath / spirit-letter, also added to Sarai → Sarah) signifies the entry of the divine name itself into Abraham's identity. Tewahedo baptismal liturgy preserves the name-given-at-baptism tradition (the newly-baptised receives a Christian saint-name) as the sacramental continuation of this Abrahamic name-change pattern.

candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis, Section XVII.10. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13, ed. J. Gwynn / Schaff (1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

Circumcision as covenant-sign in the flesh. Ephrem reads circumcision as a temporary sign pointing toward its fulfilment in baptism: the sign cut into the body of one tribe becomes the sign worked into the soul of every Christian. Tewahedo praxis preserves BOTH signs: the Tewahedo Church retains circumcision (on the 8th day for boys) as a cultural continuity with the Abrahamic covenant, while reading baptism as the salvific fulfilment — a unique Tewahedo retention that preserves the Jewish-Christian continuity Ephrem held in tension.
